summary: This note covers how the U.S. dollar is managed and issued, including the monetary base, Federal Reserve open market operations, and the debate over inflation targets. It also describes the history and design of U.S. dollar coins, from silver and Susan B. Anthony dollars to the Sacagawea and Presidential dollar coins, and how the Federal Reserve creates money when it buys securities. The dollar's international role as fiat money and reserve currency is noted.
one_line: Overview of the U.S. dollar's money supply management, Federal Reserve operations, and the history and design of U.S. dollar coins.
key_facts: The adjusted monetary base rose from approximately 400 billion dollars in 1994 to 800 billion in 2005 and over 3000 billion in 2013.
The Federal Open Market Committee, a 12-person body, meets eight times a year to determine U.S. monetary policy.
To increase the money supply, the Federal Reserve buys securities such as U.S. Treasury Bonds from banks in exchange for dollars.
The U.S. Mint introduced the $1 Presidential dollar coin in February 2007 under the Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005.
The Presidential dollar obverse features presidents in order of their inaugurations, starting with George Washington, and the reverse features the Statue of Liberty.
Grover Cleveland will appear on two Presidential dollar coins because he was the only U.S. President elected to two non-consecutive terms.
The Susan B. Anthony dollar was introduced in 1979 but proved unpopular because it was often mistaken for a quarter.
The Sacagawea dollar, introduced in 2000, has a smooth edge and a gold color and is rarely used in daily transactions.
The Kennedy half dollar was the only circulating U.S. coin with silver content from 1965 to 1970, and it was replaced with cupronickel in 1971.
The U.S. dollar is the world's most dominant reserve currency and is the currency most used in international transactions.
The British Virgin Islands and the Turks and Caicos Islands use the U.S. dollar as their sole currency.
On December 13, 2011, U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner suspended production of new Presidential dollar coins for circulation.
The Federal Reserve creates new high-powered money when it credits a seller's reserve account for a purchase.
The Treasury Department's Bureau of Engraving and Printing prints new dollar bills, and the Bureau of the Mint stamps the coins.
The experimental $4.00 Stella coin was minted in 1879 but never circulated and is considered a pattern rather than a denomination.
